rules.statement: A message broadcast between replicas to announce a change carries only an identifier as a hint, never the changed state, and each receiver re-reads the committed state from the store.
rules.why: A broadcast message may be lost, repeated or late, so it can only tell a replica to read the store; that way a replica always serves what the store committed.
rules.check: Look for broadcast/pub-sub payloads that serialize documents, settings or entity state for receivers to apply directly, instead of an identifier followed by a store read.

rules.statement: Make a post-commit refresh or change announcement best-effort: catch and log its failure, and never let it fail a write that has already committed.
rules.why: The write has committed. Polling remains the fallback for a lost notification, so failing the response would misreport the outcome.
rules.check: Look for post-commit notification, broadcast or cache-refresh calls whose exceptions propagate out of the write handler and turn a committed write into an error response.

rules.statement: Give a cache whose invalidation depends on at-most-once change notifications an absolute expiration, not a sliding one.
rules.why: A replica that misses a notification keeps a busy entry indefinitely under sliding expiration, so disabled or deleted entities stay in service. An absolute lifetime bounds how long stale state can live.
rules.check: Look for SlidingExpiration (or similar sliding options) on caches of entities that other replicas invalidate through broadcast messages, with no absolute lifetime to bound them.

rules.statement: When a subscriber may have missed change notifications (on first subscribe or on a restored connection), evict or re-read everything those notifications would have invalidated.
rules.why: Delivery is at most once. A replica that was disconnected during an announcement otherwise keeps stale cached state.
rules.check: Look for broadcast subscribers or handlers that ignore reconnect or resubscribe events, with no path that clears the cache or re-reads the store after a gap.

rules.statement: Reconcile state derived from settings by checking invariants against the current effective state, not by replaying a before/after diff captured from a write.
rules.why: Configuration reloads and deployments change effective settings without any write, so diff-driven jobs never run for them. Jobs that carry diffs also lose work on restart.
rules.check: Look for derived-state updates (key seeding, cache rebuilds, validations) that run only from a write handler's comparison of old and new documents, with nothing that handles a configuration change.

rules.statement: Run long full-scan passes in their own hosted service rather than as jobs on a shared in-process job dispatcher.
rules.why: A long pass holds the dispatcher's worker ahead of time-sensitive deliveries, and a queued job's state is lost on restart.
rules.check: Look for walks over all tenants or entities queued on a shared in-process dispatcher or job queue.

rules.statement: When a background process writes back a bookkeeping value to a row that users also write, update only that column and only if the row's concurrency token is unchanged since the process read it.
rules.why: Otherwise the background record could overwrite a concurrent user write.
rules.check: Look for background or reconciliation writes that save the whole entity, or that update without a concurrency-token condition.

rules.statement: Key a lease or deduplication marker for work driven by a state change on both the row's concurrency token and the state fingerprint, so that returning to an earlier state counts as new work.
rules.why: A fingerprint alone would skip a return to an earlier state, even though entities created in between were reconciled only against the other state.
rules.check: Look for lease or 'already processed' keys built only from a content hash or state value, with no version or concurrency token.

rules.statement: Compute a fingerprint of a settings set deterministically: order entries by name and string lists in ordinal order before hashing.
rules.why: Replicas that see the same change must produce the same fingerprint to share one lease and to recognize that there is nothing to do.
rules.check: Look for hashes over dictionaries, sets or lists that are enumerated without an explicit ordinal sort.

rules.statement: In a pass over many tenants or items, log an item that fails and continue with the next one instead of aborting the pass.
rules.why: One bad tenant must not stop reconciliation for every other tenant.
rules.check: Look for loops over tenants or entities in background passes where an exception from one item ends the whole loop, or is swallowed without being logged.

rules.statement: When a change cannot be refused (such as a configuration reload or deployment) and it invalidates stored entities, report each affected entity and its violations in a warning log, and do not refuse to start.
rules.why: Refusing to start would let one entity stop every replica and tenant. A report names the entities that will fail, which would otherwise go unnoticed.
rules.check: Look for configuration-change paths that silently leave stored entities invalid, or that throw at startup because of one invalid entity.

rules.statement: Expose a lazily built service to handlers and background services through a dependency-free singleton registry or accessor that waits until the service exists, rather than through a dependency on the services that build it.
rules.why: Background services and handlers in other packages can then reach the service without pulling in its construction graph or creating dependency cycles.
rules.check: Look for hosted services or handlers that inject a provider or factory only to get an already-materialized instance, or that build it themselves.
